subject: Volume conservation of the Leapfrog algorithm

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Volume conservation of the Leapfrog algorithm
parts:
Hi,

I am just trying to understand a few things a little better about the engine for Stan. I was wondering - I know that Neal's article on HMC says that the Leapfrog method is ''Volume conserving''. I am just wanting to check my understanding of exactly what this means.

I am assuming that we can think of probability mass as a type of incompressible flow: we want to avoid destroying or creating mass, so that we still have a valid density. 

Therefore, we need a numerical algorithm that also conserves this flow. This means that as leapfrog steps, no mass is created nor destroyed; it is merely redistributed.

Is the intuition above right, or am I way off?

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Volume conservation of the Leapfrog algorithm
parts:
Thank you, so you check the area of a circle (area=volume in 2d) is constant (using the divergence theorem, I see.) 

Also, (sorry to ask another few questions) what is the reason that Leapfrog/modified Euler are necessarily volume-conserving? Is the fact that they are reversible sufficient to show this? If so, how do you demonstrate that they are reversible? (I know that Neal states the transformations are ''shear'', which he states is enough for volume-conservation, but I was looking for a more fundamental explanation.) 

Apologies for my ignorance here. Just trying to get everything straight in my head before lecturing this stuff!

Best,

Ben
